title: Hot forming strategy for lightweight, energy-absorbing B-pillars using 7075 aluminum alloy
abstract: Abstract The article concerns the hot stamping of the B-pillar made of 7075 aluminum alloy. The first tests were carried out on a simple U-shaped element to determine the thermoplastic treatment’s parameters. Cooling the material from 475 °C to 120 °C at a cooling rate not lower than 62.8 °C/s allowed obtaining a high-strength product (above 560 MPa, hardness above 175 HV1). The determined parameters were verified while stamping the B-pillar, and the optimization of the process allowed to obtain high dimensional and shape accuracy (below 0.5 mm in critical measurement points at the parameters of pressure 0.5 and 3 MPa) and good surface quality (roughness Ra < 0.5 μm for ester oil-based lubricant for hot forming). The changes in properties were explained by TEM microstructure studies and FEM simulations.The MgZn 2  strengthening precipitates were observed during structural tests, which confirms that all heat treatment processes (solutioning and artificial aging) were performed correctly. Three-point bending tests (crashworthiness) have proved that a hot-formed aluminum pillar absorbs the same energy as a steel pillar (made of 22MnB5, currently used in automobile bodies). A ready-to-use industrial process has been developed that enables the reliable production of any components made of 7075 aluminum.
journal: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In developed countries with high environmental awareness, restrictions on fuel consumption and exhaust emissions are introduced. One of the ways to reduce exhaust fumes and carbon dioxide is to reduce vehicle weight by replacing existing body components with lighter products, most often made of light metal alloys [ 1 ]. The most crucial feature of lightweight materials is their low density and high strength, which makes them perfect for car body parts [ 2 ].

The most commonly used lightweight materials for car body parts are aluminum alloys, specifically 7075 aluminum alloy, which exhibits a tensile strength of 600 MPa in the hardened temper. The properties of 7075 alloy at elevated temperatures have been extensively researched and are well known (stress-strain curves [ 3 ,  4 ,  5 ,  6 – 7 ], FLD [ 3 ,  4 ,  6 ], structural changes [ 7 ,  8 ]). The current state of the knowledge confirms that this alloy is not suitable for forming at ambient temperature [ 9 ,  10 ]. Changes in the alloy structure occurring at elevated temperatures provide a high potential for its hot forming [ 11 ,  12 ]. Based on the stress-strain and FLD curves, it can be concluded that the optimal forming temperature is in the range of 400–510 °C. In this temperature range, the alloy-strengthening particles dissolve, resulting in high plasticity of the material [ 3 ,  4 ,  6 ]. Erdogan et al. applied 20 min of heating [ 13 ], and Atkinson et al. 10 min [ 14 ] for heat treatment, but none of them achieved the T6 temper of the final product after aging. The heated material must be transferred to cold tools and then cooled down at an appropriate rate to maintain a supersaturated temper at ambient temperature [ 15 ]. The lower the cooling rate, the greater the amount of heterogeneous precipitation [ 16 ,  17 ]. As a result, a lower cooling rate leads to a smaller volume fraction of hardening precipitates, resulting in less hardened material after aging [ 18 ]. The minimum cooling rate that ensures supersaturation of the material, according to [ 19 ] is 30 °C/s, and according to [ 20 ] is 56 °C/s, but in both cases the exact temperature of the beginning and end of the cooling was not taken into account [ 13 ,  14 ]. The authors of the manuscript noted a gap in the literature, as no one has succeeded in implementing hot-forming technology for complex high-strength products into mass production of real products. To implement this technology in the serial production of car body elements, several risks must be taken into account [ 21 ,  22 ,  23 – 24 ]. First, there is the possibility of excessive heating of the tools under continuous production conditions even when using cooling channels. Pressing sheet metal heated to 400–500 °C in continuous mode can cause local heating of the working parts of the press tool [ 25 ,  26 ]. Second, as a result of the first risk factor, the cooling rate of the formed element can be reduced, which may result in incomplete supersaturation of the material [ 27 ,  28 ].

Another problem in hot-forming processes is excessive galling of the tool’s surface and the sheet surface [ 29 ]. Due to the high temperature of the process, the problematic tribological conditions, and the high coefficient of friction between the working surfaces, a seizure of the material can occur, which in extreme cases can lead to material fracture [ 30 ,  31 ]. The resulting build-ups on the forming tool’s surface cause their accelerated wear [ 32 ]. According to research, material wear decreases with increasing forming force and punch velocity. A dense layer of oxide forms on the worn surface, slowing the rate of further wear and making adhesion the dominant wear mechanism [ 33 ]. In order to protect the tools and obtain a better sheet metal surface, a protective layer is applied to the surface of the tools, e.g. a DLC or TiN coating [ 34 ]. Research has shown that, regardless of the temperature of the semi-finished products, the DLC coating provides the lowest surface roughness of the workpiece compared to uncoated and TiN-coated tools. The discussed tests were carried out using 5182 series aluminum sheets, which were heated to 420 °C, and the tools during the tests had room temperature [ 35 ]. Recent tests with CAPVD-coated tools have reduced the adhesion of the 6082 aluminum alloy to the tools to such an extent that an 80% reduction in lubricant was possible during hot forming [ 36 ]. There are no stamping tests of 7XXX series alloys in the literature during which modern protective coatings such as TiCN and lubricants intended for hot work would be tested.

Although the state of the art has often emphasized hot forming routes for high-strength 7xxx aluminum alloys, recent work shows that warm forming should be regarded as a major alternative because intermediate temperatures can substantially improve formability while preserving, or even enhancing, the final mechanical state [ 37 ]. In particular, warm forming of AA7075 around 200 °C has been shown to reduce forming difficulty without necessarily sacrificing the T6 temper, provided that the thermal cycle is carefully controlled. Royne et al. [ 38 ] demonstrated that, for AA7075-T6, a short holding time of about 10 s at 200 °C combined with rapid heating and air quenching can prevent excessive precipitate evolution and maintain the T6 state after multi-step warm forming. Likewise, Zhang et al. [ 39 ] showed for an Al-Zn-Mg-Cu alloy that warm forming strategies can deliver improved drawability together with high post-forming hardness, highlighting that warm forming is not merely a compromise between cold and hot forming, but a process window capable of balancing deformation capability, microstructural stability, and final part performance.

Many car models (like Land Rover Defender, Ford F150, BMW series 5, E class Mercedes) use aluminum sheets only for car plating, doors, bonnets, trunks, roofs and exterior decorative elements such as moldings and bumpers. Despite repeated attempts, no one in the scientific community (Germany, Spain [ 40 ], China [ 41 ]) and industrial environment (Ford [ 42 ], Citroen 2CV0 model, Land Rover I-III series and Land Rover Defender) has managed to manufacture a B-pillar made of the 7075 alloy, which meets both the strength, quality, and safety requirements. Scientists at Huazhong University of Science & Technology in Wuhan were the first to apply the hot forming technology with and without lubricant successfully and obtained defects-free products [ 41 ]. Most of the areas of the B-pillar were within the tolerable shape deviation of ± 1 mm, but numerous local deviations exceeded ± 1 mm at both ends. The researchers focused only on the product’s geometry without testing the finished product’s strength. The 1.6 mm thick sheet metal was used, which greatly facilitated forming, but at the same time made the element less strong and less energy absorbing than a steel pillar of the same geometry and thickness. The average thickness of the steel B-pillars produced today is 1.6 mm. Due to the lower Young modulus of aluminum, the use of a 3 mm thick aluminum sheet would allow the production of a B pillar as stiff as a 1.6 mm thick steel B pillar. From the market analysis conducted by the authors, it can be concluded that there is a deep need to develop a technology to manufacture the B pillar from at least 3.0 mm thick high-strength aluminum alloy sheets.

The objective of this study was to establish an industrially applicable hot-stamping process for AA7075 aluminum alloy sheet for automotive body components and to identify the processing window that enables the manufacture of parts with the required formability, dimensional accuracy, and mechanical performance. For this purpose, the effects of heat-treatment parameters, including the temperatures defining the solution-treatment range and the minimum cooling rate (Fig.  1 ), were investigated together with the influence of tool temperature on the degree of supersaturation and the subsequent hardening response during artificial aging. Since tool temperature may increase during serial production, its effect on the stability of the process was also assessed. In addition, forming-related parameters were evaluated, including lubrication conditions and the configuration of the upper and lower presser forces, in order to obtain crack-free parts with acceptable surface quality. The process was considered successful when it produced components without cracks, local thinning, or surface scuffing, with dimensional deviations within ± 1 mm in critical mounting areas, tensile strength of at least 560 MPa (approximately 90% of the T6 condition), and energy absorption not lower than 90% of that of the corresponding 22MnB5 steel component currently used in car bodies. In this study, the comparison with boron steel was therefore used as a benchmark for the required final part performance.
Fig. 1 The diagram of the hot-forming process (with parameters to be determined)

In summary, the research results available in the literature usually concern laboratory deformation of the 7075 alloy with a thickness of 1.5 and 2.0 mm. The novelty of this article is the pressing of a complex and large geometry, which is the entire B-pillar from a 3 mm thick sheet metal in industrial conditions and its testing in three-point bending conditions, which makes the obtained results at a high of technology readiness level (TRL).

sections.heading: Heating parameters of the material
paragraphs: Based on the stress-strain, FLD curves and literature, it can be concluded that the optimal forming temperature for aluminum 7075 is in the range of 400–510 °C because of high plasticity of the material [ 13 ]. The authors of the article have designated the influence of the solutioning temperature on the final properties of the 7075 aluminum alloy sheet (to narrow the temperature range) using tensile specimens with dimensions consistent with the standard PN-EN ISO 6892-1 (Fig.  3 ). For this purpose, aluminum samples were heated to a specific temperature from the range of 425–530 °C for 45 min. The samples were placed between preheated aluminum plates in a resistance furnace. The material temperature was measured using a K-type thermocouple in the control sample. The samples were placed between preheated aluminum plates in a resistance furnace set to temperatures of 425, 450, 475, 500, 515, and 530 °C. The material temperature was measured using a K-type thermocouple in a control sample also placed between the plates. The samples were then removed using tongs and transferred to a tank of cold water and immersed (transfer time: approximately 2 s, sample cooling rate in air during transfer: 1 °C/s). Water as a cooling medium ensures the maximum cooling rate necessary to supersaturate the material - quenching with 56 °C/s. Some of the samples have been tensile tested immediately after cooling (minimum 5 pieces) on a Zwick Roel 147,800/01 tensile testing machine equipped with a force sensor with a measuring range of 0-100 kN. Strain was measured using an extensometer with an initial length of 50 mm. The strain rate was 0.001 s − 1 . The remaining part of samples was artificially aged in a resistance furnace at 120 °C for 8 h. Aged samples have been also tensile tested and their hardness was measured using the Vickers method with an indenter load of 1 kg. The heat treatment and tensile test parameters are shown in Table  3 .

sections.heading: Forming tools
paragraphs: U-shape production tests are performed to quickly compare various sheet metal materials and to determine technological parameters such as deformability, springback, susceptibility to seizures, cracks and other defects. The U-shape is similar to the central part of the B pillar, and technological tests of the U production made it possible to determine parameters such as the cooling rate and final temperature of the blank in conditions similar to the serial production of the entire pillar. Technological tests were conducted at the University (laboratory) using a die designed and manufactured by industrial company KIRCHHOFF Polska Sp.z o.o. (Fig.  4 a) mounted on the AKO 360-200T hydraulic press with a maximum pressure of 2000 kN and a working area of 1000 × 1000 × 1000 mm. The tools have holes for mounting cartridge heaters used during forming at elevated temperatures, up to a maximum of 400 °C. The forming elements are made of 1.2738HH improved alloy steel with a low thermal expansion. Due to the appropriately selected chemical composition, high purity of the manufacturing process, special heat treatment, and fine microstructure, it is characterized by an excellent polishing capability, high surface quality, and a very high degree of uniformity of mechanical properties (e.g. hardness and impact toughness) across the entire cross-section. In addition, all forming elements (dies and punches) were surface hardened by thermo-chemical nitriding, and a special CrN (chromium nitride) coating, resistant to abrasion at high temperatures, was applied.
Fig. 4 U-shaped element ( a ) tools mounted on the hydraulic press, ( b ) tensile specimens location and position of K-type thermocouples

The input material for test were the 400 × 200 mm rectangular samples laser cut from AA7075 sheets. The edges of each sample were ground to remove burrs. Three k-type thermocouples were installed inside blind holes (∅1.2 × 15 mm) drilled in the blank (Fig.  4 b) before starting the experiment. The visible crack was local, occurred after the pressing process and had no influence on its course.

sections.heading: Research procedure
paragraphs: The blank was held for 45 min in a furnace preheated to 495 °C (± 5 °C) to allow for supersaturation from the initial temperature of 475 °C, in order to dissolve the precipitates and obtain a homogeneous microstructure. The temperature difference results from the manual transfer of the blank from the furnace to the forming tools and its cooling in the air during that time. Next, the hot blank was transferred from the furnace to the tools preheated to a temperature of 50, 70, 90, 120, 180, 210, and 230 °C. The transfer time lasted 15–20 s, and the sheet was formed by the stamp moving at a federate of 14 mm/s. The closing time of the tools was 5 s. The shaped and supersaturated products were then aged in an oven at 120 °C for 8 h.The detailed parameters of the shaping process are presented in Table  4 .

Table 4 Forming process parameters Process Parameter Value Forming Feedrate 14 mm/s Lubricant Multidraw SHF 431 (ester oil based) Maximum pressure 200 bar Tool temperature 21, 50, 70, 90, 120, 150, 180, 210, 230 °C Solutioning Temperature 475 °C Time 45 min Aging Temperature 120 °C Time 8 h

sections.heading: Testing of finished components – U-shape
paragraphs: Specimens for tensile testing (Fig.  3 ) were cut out from the places marked in Fig.  4 b. The tests were carried out with an initial strain rate of 10 − 3  s − 1 . Before tensile testing, the hardness of the samples was examined using the LECO hardness tester. For this purpose, the gripping parts of the specimens were used. The experiment was carried out according to the PN-EN ISO 6507-1 standard using the HV1 scale. At least five indentations were made in each measurement area and the mean value was calculated.

sections.heading: Thermodynamic and kinetic calculations
paragraphs: To quantitatively analyze the potential precipitation of 7075 alloy resulting from thermoplastic treatment, thermodynamic and kinetic simulations were conducted in MatCalc. Precipitation were treated with a size-class precipitation model based on the numerical Kampmann–Wagner approach. The simulation is carried out in a mean-field precipitation domain - the matrix was assumed homogeneous within the representative volume element, with homogeneous temperature, pressure, and composition in that domain. Precipitates were described through size classes, each defined by radius, number density, and composition, and it reports outputs such as phase fraction and mean precipitate radius. The composition of the analyzed alloy was determined in the program according to Table  2 , with aluminum as the base element of the matrix. The temperature curves determined in Chap. 3.2.1 (Fig.  5 ) were used as the temperature characteristics of the heat treatment of the analyzed alloy. The modeled initial state corresponded to the supersaturated solid solution after solution treatment. The simulations were performed with an assumed deformation of 0.3, which corresponds to the actual deformations in critical areas of the extrusion (e.g. on the lateral wall). The simulation work will help to link the alloy’s chemical composition with heat treatment parameters and microstructure (phase and particle proportions, and PFZ layer width), which directly affects the material’s strength.
Fig. 5  Forming tools ( a ) arrangement of cooling channels, ( b ) tools installed on the press

sections.heading: FEM simulations
paragraphs: In order to determine the preliminary parameters of the deep drawing process (the force values of the upper and lower dies) and to explain the reasons for the differences in mechanical strength between different areas of the 7075 aluminum alloy blank (side—the most deformed area, flange—the least deformed area), numerical simulations of the hot forming process were performed in the MSC.MARC software using the Implicite method, which was employed to carry out thermomechanical calculations. The punch and die tools were assumed to be rigid and non-deformable. Furthermore, the following boundary conditions were assumed: Poisson’s ratio 0.33 at ambient temperature (for hot stamping simulations the coefficient assumed for calculations is 0.26), Young’s modulus of 0.7 GPa, contact heat transfer coefficient from 1.5 kW/(m 2 *K) for 0 MPa to 4 kW/(m 2 *K) for 2 MPa, bilinear Coulumb friction model, and friction coefficient of 0.3. Shell-solid finite elements were used. To simplify the model and shorten calculation time, the lower part of the B-pillar, containing two critical areas—the flange and the side, was analyzed. According to preliminary analyses, the B-pillar foot is the most complex pillar geometry and it is in this part that the greatest concentration of deformations occurs.

The material model was assumed to be elastic-plastic (Mises) and isotropic, dependent on strain, strain rate, and temperature (σ (ε, έ, T)). The elastic part was assumed as a linear relationship, and the plastic part as the hardening curves from tensile tests (yielding stress – true plastic strain relationship). The authors determined stress-strain curves for temperatures of 21, 100, 200, 230, 300, 350, 400, 420, and 500 °C and strain rates of 0.001, 0.01, and 0.1 s –1 . The elastic range was removed from the obtained curves, and then extrapolation was performed using mathematical tools in MATLAB. This allowed to determine the hardening curves at the tested temperatures for larger strains and extrapolate the results for higher strain rates (up to 1000 s − 1 ) needed to simulate the hot forming process of 7075 aluminum sheet. Data was entered in the form of points for the assumed plastic strains, strain rates, and temperatures. A maximum tool pressure of 200 tons was assumed (corresponding to the pressure of a hydraulic press), and the maximum ram speed was 14 mm/s with rapid approach to the press’s working position.

sections.heading: Forming tools
paragraphs: Verification of material tests and optimal forming parameters obtained during stamping trials of the U-shaped element was performed during hot stamping of the entire B-pillar. For this purpose, specially designed tools were manufactured of 1.2738HH alloy steel (the same grade of steel as U-shape tools). The working surface of the tools was covered with a 2.5 μm thick TiCN layer with a hardness of 2400 HV0.025. The tools can be actively cooled below 21 °C by the cold medium flowing through cooling channels (Fig.  6 a). The stamping tools were mounted on a hydraulic press with a maximum pressure of 500 tons in the hall of an industrial company (Fig.  6 b). Additionally, the tools were equipped with 18 thermocouples to register temperature in individual die sectors.
Fig. 6 The location of specimens used for tensile and hardness testing

sections.heading: Research procedure
paragraphs: The first stamping tests of the B-pillar were carried out following the parameters used during forming of the U-shaped element (Table  4 ). The blank edges were polished, and K-type thermocouples were installed inside the holes drilled on the blank side. This approach allowed for monitoring the sheet temperature determining the time necessary to obtain the solutioning temperature and control that the temperature of the sheet metal at the moment of shaping and solution heat treatment is not lower than the designated value of 475 °C. The process was carried out under 10 strokes/min, which was close to the stroke rate used in the industrial practice for stamping car body parts. The detailed process parameters are presented in Table  5 .

Table 5 Process parameters for stamping the B-pillar Process Parameter Value Forming Feedrate 10 strokes/min Lubricant Multidraw SHF 431 Maximum pressure 500 tons Tool temperature 21 °C Pressure of the upper die 5, 50, 100, 150 bar Pressure of the lower die 30, 50 bar Solutioning Temperature 475 °C Time 45 min Aging Temperature 120 °C Time 8 h

The clamping parameters directly impact the material’s behavior during forming, and they largely determine the input shape of the sheet. Due to the small roundings of the tools, high pressure will result in increased uniaxial stretching and compression of the material, which may result in a loss of stability. Properly selected input shape of the sheet can reduce the drawing of the material and prevent it from cracking or excessive thinning.

sections.heading: Strength tests and hardness measurement
paragraphs: Strength and hardness tests were carried out using specimens (Fig.  3 ) cut out from the final product’s selected location (Fig.  7 ). In each of the areas presented, six samples were extracted: three dog-bone specimens for tensile testing and three rectangular specimens for hardness testing. The selected areas have different contact times with the working surface of the tools and, thus, different cooling rates.
Fig. 7 Test stand for 3-point bending of B pillars ( a ) model, ( b ) diagram

sections.heading: Microstructure evaluation
paragraphs: The microstructure of individual areas of the B-pillar was carefully examined using an electron microscope. The test specimens were cut out from the areas where the risk of material under-saturation is the highest due to the short contact time of the blank and tools (flange and lateral – Fig.  7 ).

From the longitudinal section of the samples, thin foils were prepared on both sides (from the top and bottom), grinding and then electropolishing using the TenuPol-5 automatic electrolytic polishing machine and cutting with a special guillotine sample ø3 mm. The electrolytic thinning process was carried out in the reagent with 330 ml HNO3 + 660 ml methanol CH3OH until the hole was in the central part of the sample.

Observations of the tested samples after various heat or thermo-mechanical treatments were carried out using transmission electron microscope (TEM) TECNAI G20 X Twin with EDS adapter and HAADF detector. Chemical analysis and point diffraction were used to identify phases in the tested alloys. Point diffraction was solved using Sleeve 4 + software using the PDF4 + database.

sections.heading: Shape deviation testing
paragraphs: The 7520si ROMER Absolute measuring arm was used for the contactless measurement of finished products. The shape deviation was determined using the “best fit” method by comparing the scanned geometry of the B-pillar and the CAD model. The maximum shape deviation of ± 1 mm was set as the geometry acceptance criterion. The mentioned value is commonly used in the automotive industry for the geometry evaluation of car body elements. Particular attention was paid to the most important measurement points related to the process of assembly the pillar to the car body.

The advantage of the patented stand is that it enables repeatable comparative testing of complete B-pillars without the need to destroy an entire vehicle. The method does not replace full-vehicle crash tests required for homologation, but it provides an effective way to compare the relative crashworthiness and energy absorption potential of different B-pillar concepts before vehicle-level validation.Mounting the station on a hydraulic press and using the slider drive allows tests to be performed in quasi-static conditions (the impactor’s movement speed was 1 mm/s).

sections.heading: Supersaturation parameters of the material
paragraphs: The results of strength tests are presented in the graph in Fig.  9 . Each measurement point is the average value of all tests for a given solution temperature (minimum of 5 tests). The deviation of the results from the mean value was so small that it is invisible on the graph (max. 3%, values smaller than the plotted measurement points). Based on the graph, it was observed that four temperature ranges can be distinguished based on the obtained results. In the temperature range of 425–450 °C the material strengthened (an increase of 71 and 63%, respectively) in the strength in the aged state, compared to the supersaturated state. However, only in the temperature range of 475–500 °C provides the most heterogeneous results and allows obtaining favorable mechanical properties similar to the T6 temper (strength above 560 MPa, above 90% of the value in T6 condition). No precipitation hardening was observed if the temperature was above 515 °C (no difference between hardness after solution heat treatment and hardness after aging). Samples supersaturated at 530 °C cracked brittle in the measurement area. The crack location was examined under a light microscope, and the obtained metallographic section is shown in Fig.  10 .
Fig. 9 Intercrystalline cracks caused by molten eutectic
Fig. 10 Temperature change of the material during forming of the U-shaped blank

A similar relationship as in Fig.  9  for 7075 alloy was determined by Liu et al. [ 43 ]. Except that the above authors determined the dependence of the change in HV hardness on the supersaturation temperature immediately after supersaturation of the material. In contrast, the present publication determined the material’s strength both immediately after supersaturation and after artificial aging, which complements the results. As the temperature of the solution increased, both hardness and strength after water quenching first increased and then decreased. In both cases, a similar temperature range was tested: 425–530 °C vs. 430–550 °C.

The observed crack (Fig.  10 ) is an intercrystalline crack caused by overheating of the material in the furnace during the solution process. According to [ 7 ], the temperature of 530 °C caused the eutectic to melt, which in turn could have caused crystallization of the eutectic at the grain boundaries of the α solid solution. However, according to the authors’ current knowledge, eutectics are not present in 7075 alloys (in the same sense as, for example, 4xxx series alloys). These phases often form at grain boundaries due to the accumulation of defects and lower-melting phases/elements, such as MgZn 2 , at this point.

High temperatures during solution heat treatment of precipitation-strengthened aluminum alloys are necessary to dissolve Mg and Zn in the aluminum matrix. Both elements dissolve in the aluminum in the solid state. Diffusion processes then occur. Subsequently, during alloy cooling, the phase change process is halted at the level of dissolution of the matrix components. However, if the cooling process is prolonged or gradual, nucleation will occur. Cr accelerates nucleation because it is highly melting and will attract Zn and Mg, which will then accumulate on it. The less Mg and Zn dissolved in the matrix (because they will be in phases with Cr), the less the aging effect will be.The temperature of 475 °C was selected as the optimal temperature - it is high enough to achieve the T6 temper and prevents from melting of the eutectic. Therefore, solutioning start temperature of the material during testing of the U-shaped element (p. 3.2) and the entire B-pillar (p. 3.3) was set to 475 °C and the heating time should be longer than 45 min.

sections.heading: Temperature measurement
paragraphs: Figure  5  shows the cooling curves recorded using a thermocouple placed on the front surface of the U-shape (as shown in Fig.  4 b). The all curves were divided into four areas characterized by the different cooling rates of the material. The first range from 0 to 7 s is the final phase of the material heating stage in the furnace at a constant, set temperature of 495 ± 5 °C. The second range lasting from 7 to 26 s includes the furnace’s opening, transportation of the blank on the tool’s surface and beginning of forming (a decrease in temperature to 460–475 °C). In this range, the blank’s temperature decrease is primarily caused by convection and radiation between its upper surface and the air, and the contact heat transfer between the lower surface and the lower die. The third range (from 26 to 31 s) represents forming until the die is completely closed (circa 200 °C). In this range, the sheet metal is cooled by contact with the surface of the steel tools, but this contact is uneven, usually linear, because the sheet metal is not pressed against the surface of the tools. The fourth range, from 31 to 34 s represents holding the sheet in closed tools. After the die is closed, the hot blank and the tools are in full contact under high pressure, and the contact heat transfer coefficient is much higher than the convection and radiation coefficient, which causes the temperature of the blank to drop rapidly.
Fig. 11 Influence of the initial temperature of the tools on the cooling rate of 7075 aluminum alloy

As observed in the Fig.  11 , the cooling rate of the sheet decreases with the increase of the die temperature. The initial tool’s temperature below 120 °C guarantees that the sheet’s cooling speed will not be lower than 62,8 °C/s. According to the authors’ research, it should theoretically result in obtaining a supersaturated state of the material after cooling it to temperature below 200 °C. This should allow for reaching the initial hardness of T6 temper after further artificial aging (when the cooling rate is at least 30–56 °C/s) [ 19 ,  44 ]. However, the condition of the material also depends on the initial and final temperature during forming, which varies in different element regions. Therefore, further tests are necessary (tensile tests, hardness measurements, and structure tests).

The determined cooling rates were very similar to those obtained by Zhang et al. [ 45 ]. For tool temperatures of 25 and 90–100 °C, the cooling rate was at a similar level, approximately 120 °C/s and approximately 72–79 °C/s, respectively. For the tool temperature range of 120–150 °C, the difference in the obtained hardnesses did not exceed 10%, for the range of 180–200 °C it was 23%.

sections.heading: Strength tests and hardness measurement
paragraphs: The influence of the initial temperature of the tools on the finished products’ strength and hardness (after the supersaturation, forming and artificial aging is presented in Fig.  12  along with the standard deviation of the obtained values. Each value in the graph is the average value of three measurement locations (front, lateral, flange) from at least three trials for each tool temperature tested.
Fig. 12 Strength and hardness of the U-shape after thermo-plastic treatment

Based on Fig.  12 , it can be concluded that heating the tools’ to a temperature of up to 90 °C does not adversely affect the supersaturation of the material. The strength of the final product formed in the tools with a temperature of (21–90)°C and artificially aged exceeded 555 MPa, which means that the material was fully oversaturated during forming. The strength of the drawpieces formed in tools hotter than 90 °C gradually decreases. The measured hardness of the materials confirmed this observation. The material strength decreases from 548 MPa for tools’ temperature of 120 °C to 450 MPa for tools’ temperature of 230 °C. This phenomenon is associated with an incomplete supersaturation of the 7075 aluminum alloy before the hot-forming process.

A similar study was conducted by Zhang et al. [ 45 ], but the preparation they used had a smaller thickness (2 mm) and a smaller surface area (150 × 140 mm). Comparing the same or similar forming tool temperatures, the following HV hardness values were obtained: 185 vs. 173 (for 25 °C), 150 vs. 173 (for 90–100 °C), 139 vs. 165 (for 150–180 °C), 125 vs. 139 (for 200–210 °C) and 155 vs. 132 (for 230–250 °C). Comparing the value of actual stresses (after conversion by the authors, in MPa), the following was obtained: 633 vs. 616 (for 25 °C), 626 vs. 616 (for 90–100 °C), 613 vs. 592 (for 150–180 °C), 585 vs. 523 (for 200–210 °C) and 514 vs. 500 (for 230–250 °C).

The tool’s temperature equal to 21–180 °C allows reaching a cooling rate greater than 30 °C/s during the forming phase of the U-shaped element. This means that the state of a supersaturated material should theoretically be achieved. However, tensile tests and hardness measurements demonstrated that only samples made with tools colder than 90 °C were adequately supersaturated - their strength (> 560 MPa) and hardness (> 169 HV1) were close to the strength and hardness of T6 temper. For tools heated above 90 °C, the strength and hardness of the formed elements decreased progressively. This indicates that the cooling rate alone is not sufficient to evaluate the supersaturation effectiveness; the initial blank temperature, final forming temperature, tool temperature, and local contact conditions must also be considered. Tools with temperatures of 210 and 230 °C resulted in cooling rates of 24 and 21 °C/s, respectively, which were insufficient to suppress precipitation during cooling. As a result, incomplete supersaturation occurred, leading to reduced strengthening after artificial aging. Based on these results, the maximum permissible tool temperature during hot forming of 7075 aluminum alloy was defined as 90 °C. Therefore, during continuous production, the tool temperature should be monitored to verify whether repeated contact with sheet metal heated to 400–500 °C causes local overheating of the working surfaces. If the tool temperature exceeds 90 °C, an additional cooling system should be applied to maintain the required heat-transfer conditions.

sections.heading: Thermodynamic and kinetic calculations
paragraphs: Figure  13  shows the change in the mean precipitate radius as a function of time (dashed line). Figure  14  shows the volume fraction of precipitates in the microstructure as a function of time (dashed line). Both graphs also show the change in material temperature depending on the temperature of the forming tools (continuous line), which enabled analysis and explanation of phase changes in the context of the change in material temperature.
Fig. 13 Predicted mean precipitate radius in the microstructure and the temperature of the material as a function of time
Fig. 14 Predicted volume fraction of precipitates in the microstructure and the temperature of the material as a function of time

Based on the calculated graphs, it can be observed that within the material cooling range (from 500 to approximately 300 °C), no changes occur in the material structure. This temperature range encompasses the process of removing the material from the furnace, transferring it to the tools, and initiating shaping. Only when the tools first contact the material does a significant temperature drop occur (at a high cooling rate), initiating phase changes. When the tools are in full contact with the material and the alloy temperature drops below 200 °C, the simulation predicts a maximum mean precipitate radius of approximately 5 nm together with a phase fraction of about 0.05. This pattern of curves occurs for tool temperatures in the range of 20–120 °C, due to the sufficiently high cooling rate of the alloy to below 200 °C. The curves preticted for tool temperatures in the range of 210–230 °C have a different characteristic. The first appearance of precipitates (with an average radius of approximately 4 nm) occurs during the first contact of the tools with the material (material temperature drops below 350 °C). Only then, a drop in temperature below 250 °C causes the radius to increase to 12 nm with a phase fraction of 0.04.

The presented graphs allowed for the analysis of changes during the individual forming stages (opening the furnace, transferring the extrusion to the tools, shaping, closing the tools). On this basis, the influence of the cooling tool temperature on the mean precipitate radius and phase fraction was calculated - Fig.  15 . These results indicate that tool temperature affects both the kinetics of precipitation and the final precipitate state during forming.
Fig. 15 Changes in the mean precipitate radius and proportion of precipitates depending on the temperature of the shaping tools

sections.heading: FEM simulations
paragraphs: Figure  16  shows the effect of the forces exerted by the upper and lower blankholder on the distribution of major and minor strains in the sheet metal blank. In all analyzed cases, it can be observed that the highest concentration of principal strains occurs on the side surface of the stamping, between the front and the flange (areas marked in green in Fig.  16 a, b, c, and d - figures on the left). This is due to the fact that in these areas the material experiences the greatest deformation, and that the upper and lower blankholders hold the material from the top (front surface) and from the bottom (flange), which generates resistance to the material’s movement. Furthermore, the fact that deformation occurs at a high initial sheet temperature (475 °C) increases the coefficient of friction between the tool surface and the material, creating additional resistance even with the use of lubricant. The highest strain values occurred for lower and upper blankholder settings of 5/15 and 5/10 MPa - strains of -0.25 and − 0.28, respectively - and are concentrated in a small area. In contrast, in the other two cases (blankholder settings of 3/5 and 3/0.5 MPa), the strain levels reach − 0.21 and − 0.16, covering a larger area, which makes the strain distribution more uniform and favorable. A similar relationship holds for minor strain – for blankholder settings of 5/15 and 5/10 MPa, the strains equal 0.8 and 0.54, and are concentrated in a small area, while for settings of 3/5 and 3/0.5, they decrease to 0.45 and 0.41 and are more widespread and uniform. In turn, Fig.  17  shows the distribution of sheet thinning. As with strains, as the blankholder force decreases, the maximum sheet thinning decreases and the thinning becomes more uniform. For blankholder settings of 5/15 MPa, the minimum sheet thickness is 2.19 mm; this value then increases to the range of 2.45–2.47 mm for settings of 5/10 and 3/5 MPa, up to 2.57 mm for settings of 3/0.5 MPa.

Fig. 16 Strain distribution during hot forming of the lower part of the B-pillar (left) major strain, (right) minor strain: ( a ) p lower  = 5 MPa, p upper  = 15 MPa, ( b ) p lower  = 5 MPa, p upper  = 10 MPa, ( c ) p lower  = 3 MPa, p upper  = 5 MPa, ( d ) p lower  = 3 MPa, p upper  = 0.5 MPa

Fig. 17 Distribution of thickness and during hot forming of the lower part of the B-pillar : ( a ) p lower  = 5 MPa, p upper  = 15 MPa, ( b ) p lower  = 5 MPa, p upper  = 10 MPa, ( c ) p lower  = 3 MPa, p upper  = 5 MPa, ( d ) p lower  = 3 MPa, p upper  = 0.5 MPa

sections.heading: Manufacturing of the B-pillar
paragraphs: Due to the much larger blank size (compared to forming a U-shaped element), stamping the entire B-pillar involved adjusting the selected parameters of thermo-plastic treatment (initial and final temperature of the blank, strain rate). Additionally, the tools were equipped with 18 thermocouples to register temperature in individual die sectors. There are 7 measurement points in the punch area (points 1.1–1.7 in Table  6 ), 3 measurement points in the blank holder (points 2.1–2.3), and 8 measurement points in the die (points 3.1–3.8). To protect the thermocouples from damage during sheet metal forming, they are routed to the measurement points through internal channels ending just below the tool surface (approximately 4–5 mm from the tool’s outer surface). Table  6  shows the temperature distribution of the tools measured at the beginning of the test, during the middle series (after 30 pieces) and the final series (after 60 pieces). The blankholder is the first component to absorb heat from the hot blank because it is the first to come into contact with the hot sheet metal during the initial stage of stamping. In addition, the blankholder operates at a set pressure (ranging from 0.5 to 15 MPa), which accelerates the heat absorption process. During tests of the entire pillar, the temperature of the presser—which is a separate component of the tool (die)—was measured, and its temperature reached a maximum of 39.4 °C (measurement points 2.1–2.3 in Table  6 ). It means that the maximum permissible value of temperature of the tools determined in the Chap. 3.2.2. was not exceeded (90 °C) during hot forming process. Therefore it is assumed that the tools do not require any specialized cooling system.

Figure  18 a depicts one of the first drawpieces that was supersaturated at 500 °C for 45 min. The pressure of the lower blankholder was 5 MPa and the upper 15 MPa. The temperature of the sheet just before stamping was 477 °C. The element cracked in three places marked in Fig.  18 a – in the upper part and in the radius. This is consistent with the FEM simulations performed, because it is in the transition area between the front and the side that the stress concentration occurs (Figs.  16  and  17 ). In the next step, the upper pressure was reduced to 10, then to 5 MPa and pressure of the lower blankholder to 3 MPa according to the recommendations of FEM simulations, which resulted in a reduction of cracks (Fig.  18 b).
Fig. 18 Stamping results ( a ) the first drawpiece (p lower  = 5 MPa, p upper  = 15 MPa), ( b ) the next drawpiece (p lower  = 3 MPa, p upper  = 5 MPa)

The summary of the tested blankholders settings and the obtained results is presented in Table  7 . Reducing pressure of the upper blankholder set to 5 bar allowed to produce crack-free drawpieces (Fig.  19 ). Reducing the pressure of the upper blankholder from 15 MPa to 0.5 MPa and that of the lower blankholder from 5 MPa to 3 MPa reduced the restriction of material flow in the flange area and promoted more uniform material deformation toward the bottom of the die. As a result, the concentration of deformation on the radius between the side wall and the end face of the blank was reduced. In the simulation with p upper  = 15 MPa and p lower  = 5 MPa, the greatest plastic deformation occurred in the same areas where cracks were experimentally observed. After reducing the press pressure to p upper  = 0.5 MPa and p lower  = 3 MPa, the maximum deformation was lower, and the deformation field became more uniform, which was consistent with the experimentally obtained column B without cracks. The determined forming parameters allowed for a series of tests to produce B-pillars in continuous mode without cracks.

Table 7 Configuration of the tested presser settings Pressure of the upper blankholder [MPa] Pressure of the lower blankholder [MPa] Visual evaluation of the drawpiece 15 5 Cracks on the radius in the foot area of the pillar and in the head area (Fig.  16 a) 10 5 Cracks on the radius in the foot area of the pillar 5 3 Crack in the head area of the pillar (Fig.  16 b) 0.5 3 A defect-free drawpiece (Fig.  19 )
Fig. 19 The drawpiece without cracks (p lower  = 3 MPa, p upper  = 0.5 MPa)

In Fig.  19 , arrows mark three areas on the lateral surface of the B-pillar where surface roughness was measured using a Mitutoyo SJ-210 roughness meter. Measurements were taken from the side visible in Fig.  19  and from the other, invisible side (total 6 measurement points). The average R a  roughness value was below 0.5 μm achieved during forming trials using a synthetic lubricant based on ester oil, commercially known as Multidraw SHF 431, designed for deep drawing of aluminum alloys at elevated temperatures (above 300 °C - EN ISO 2592), with a manufacturer-proprietary composition. Lubricant characteristics - physical state: liquid, relative density: 0.93 g/cm3, kinematic viscosity: 350 mm 2 /s (ASTM D 7042). The acceptable R a  roughness value for the automotive industry (below 1 μm) was obtained during hot forming the B-pillar with using Multidraw SHF 431.

Due to the much larger blank size, the initial furnace temperature was set to 500 °C and the holding time was extended to 45 min to ensure a homogeneous temperature distribution throughout the entire blank. The minimum solutioning start temperature was assumed to be 475 °C. Since the air-cooling rate of aluminum is approximately 1–2 °C/s, the transfer time of the blank should not exceed 10–15 s. Longer transfer times may reduce the blank temperature below the range required for effective forming and supersaturation (475 °C). During B-pillar forming trials and continuous production tests, the tools made of 1.2738HH steel did not exceed the maximum permissible temperature of 90 °C. Therefore, under the tested conditions, no additional specialized cooling system was required. However, this condition should be verified for industrial-scale production, where longer production runs may cause higher local tool temperatures. The forming trials also showed that cracking and wrinkling could be eliminated by optimizing the blankholder pressures. The best results were obtained using a lower blankholder pressure of 3 MPa and an upper blankholder pressure of 0.5 MPa, which allowed more uniform material flow and reduced strain concentration in the lateral and head areas of the pillar.

sections.heading: Strength tests and hardness measurement
paragraphs: The finished B-pillars were aged at 120 °C for 8 h to regain T6 temper properties. Next, the strength and hardness of crucial areas were measured, and the average values are depicted in Fig.  20 .
Fig. 20 Strength properties and microstructure of the B-pillar in crucial areas at risk of non-saturation of the material

Strength varies depending on the area studied. The slight differences result from the different contact times of the given areas (flange, side, head, foot) with the cold tools (cooling starts and ends at different times). First, the front surface of the foot and the head come into contact with the tools. The areas mentioned have an ultimate tensile strength above 577 MPa. This results from the highest cooling rate and initial temperature of the material before the cooling begins. The flange is formed in the next step. Its strength is equal to 567–573 MPa. Finally, the side surfaces of the B-pillar are stamped. Their strength is 565 MPa. All areas of the B-pillar have ultimate tensile strength above 560 MPa, which qualifies the product as a car body element [ 46 ].

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: The microstructural observations revealed the presence of different types of phases within the grains (Fig.  21 ). No Guinier–Preston (GP) zones or η′ (eta prime) precipitates were detected. Instead, relatively coarse particles were observed both within the grain interiors and along the grain boundaries, where they appeared elongated or partially coalesced. The size of these particles ranged from 50 to 300 nm.
Fig. 21 TEM images in bright field ( a ) and ( b ) for the sample taken from the flange part, and ( c ) and ( d ) for the sample taken from the lateral with a rounded part

Quantitative image analysis of the TEM micrographs revealed differences in the phase surface fraction and average particle area between the two samples. Sample taken from the flange area exhibited a significantly higher phase fraction (28%) compared to sample taken from lateral (6%). Furthermore, the average particle area in flange was approximately 1.2 μm², which is twice the average value measured in lateral (0.6 μm²). In both samples, a precipitation-free zone (PFZ) of approximately 100 nm was identified along the grain boundaries.

Phase identification was carried out by combining selected area electron diffraction (SAED) and micro-area EDS analysis. In sample from flange, bright-field (BF), SAED, and scanning TEM (STEM) imaging coupled with line and point EDS analyses (Fig.  22 ) confirmed that the primary phase present was MgZn₂ or a chemically equivalent phase, (Cu, Zn, Al)₂Mg, consistent with literature data [ 47 ]. The surrounding matrix in the analysed regions showed only aluminium, indicating a lack of solute segregation or fine-scale precipitation.

Fig. 22 TEM analysis of a sample taken from the flange in ( a ) bright field image (BF), ( b ) selected area electron diffraction pattern (SAED) together with phase analysis of MgZn 2  based on ( c ) linear chemical analysis and ( d ) point chemical analysis in selected areas of EDS, STEM

In contrast, the analysis of sample from lateral revealed the presence of a different intermetallic compound identified as phase E (Al₁₈Mg₃Cr₂), commonly formed during homogenisation treatment [ 48 ], as shown in Fig.  23 . Spot EDS analysis (Fig.  23 c) also indicated the coexistence of η (MgZn₂) and θ (Al₂Cu) phases within the area occupied by phase E. The presence of the θ-phase was further confirmed through SAED pattern analysis and point EDS at location 2 (Fig.  24 ), consistent with findings reported by Abolfazl Azarniya. Despite the presence of coarse intermetallic phases, neither GP zones nor η′ precipitates were detected in either sample. The absence of fine-scale precipitation was further confirmed by the lack of detectable solute elements in the matrix during micro-area EDS analysis (Fig.  24 c). Cu and Al atoms can be dissolved in η phase substituting for Zn atoms at the Zn sublattice to form a quaternary phase of (Cu, Zn, Al) 2 Mg, which is isomorphous with MgZn 2 .

Fig. 23 TEM analysis of a sample taken from the lateral in ( a ) bright field image (BF), ( b ) selected area electron diffraction pattern (SAED) together with phase analysis of Al 18 Mg 3 Cr 2  based on ( c ) point chemical analysis in selected areas of EDS, STEM

Fig. 24 TEM analysis of a sample taken from the lateral in ( a ) bright field image (BF), ( b ) selected area electron diffraction pattern (SAED) together with phase analysis of Al 2 Cu based on ( c ) point chemical analysis in selected areas of EDS, STEM

sections.heading: Shape deviation
paragraphs: The finished B-pillar was optically scanned before and after it was cut to its final shape. Figure  25  depicts the geometric deviation calculated by comparing the final part scan with its geometrical model.
Fig. 25 Geometric deviation of the the finished B-pillar ( a ) before trimming,  b ) after trimming

The geometric deviation of the B-pillar improved after trimming. The geometric deviation of one point in the middle area is 0.73 mm and the other measuring points are within the tolerance range (less than 0.5 mm). All points in the head area are below ± 0.5 mm. Only two measuring points in the foot area exceed the permissible deviation (points 23 and 30: values 1.55 and 1.63 may result from handling the material with pliers while transferring the sample from the furnace to the stamping station). Further reduction of the shape deviations is related to the constructional correction of tools, e.g., increasing the radius of the die and automation of the process so that the blank is transported utilizing a neutral method. Figure  25  shows the critical measurement points related to mounting the pillar to the car body (no. 28, 12 and 10) - all marked points are within the permissible deviation range of ± 0.5 mm.

sections.heading: Crash test
paragraphs: Figure  26  shows a graph of force versus deflection recorded during the three-point compression testing of B-pillars. The graph displays two curves (blue and purple) representing the compression of a pillar made of 3-mm-thick 7075 aluminum sheet, manufactured according to the forming method described in Sect.  3.3.2. (annealing the blank at 475 °C, forming in room-temperature dies, artificial aging at 120 °C for 8 h). Additionally, bending tests were conducted on two pillars made of 1.5 mm thick 22MnB5 manganese-boron steel sheet. These pillars were manufactured using the hot forming method (annealing the blank at the austenitizing temperature of 950 °C for at least 5 min, forming and quenching in ambient-temperature dies with a critical cooling rate of approximately 27 °C/s). Full martensitic transformation in the material results in an increase in tensile strength to 1500 MPa. Currently, this is the standard technology for stamping steel components for automotive bodies [ 49 ].
Fig. 26 Force-deflection diagram determined during 3-point bendig of the B-pillar

Based on the force-displacement graph (Fig.  26 ) three main deformation stages can be distinguished during quasi-static bending of the B pillar’s made of both aluminum and high-strength steel. Analysing the proportional part of the force-deflecion curve (for the deflecion ranging from 0 to 15 mm) led to a conclusion that aluminum element was charactesied by about 60% higher stiffness. Application of 20 kN bending force resulted in 15 mm deflection of steel part, while 32 kN was needed to reach the same deflection of aluminum part.

In the second phase (15–40 mm steel; 15–60 mm aluminum) plastic deformations occur and the B pillar wraps deforms severily. Comparing both materials it can be noted that, the steel element loses stability faster than the aluminum one. Crushing force of steel element is increasing monotonically up to 40 mm. Next the force is decreasing and the extensive cracking in the middle part may be observed. This result from the lower deformation at break A50 of 22MnB5 steel (6–8%) comparing to T6 temper of 7075 aluminum alloy (10–12%). Contrary, the aluminum elements, are in contact up to the deflection of 60 mm. It may also be noted that the aluminum element deforms mostly plastically without losing stability (Fig.  27 b), while the steel b-pillar is breaking in central area as depicted in Fig.  27 a. Additionally, the maximum crushing force was about 32% higher in case of aluminum element (50 kN for aluminum element; 38 kN for steel element).
Fig. 27 The deformation mode after 54 mm deflection geometric deviation ( a ) steel pillar, ( b ) aluminum pillar
In the 3rd stage both b-pillars have already lost stability and the use of fixed supports results in the increase of the tensile force.

The force–deflection curves obtained for the steel and aluminum B-pillars show a similar overall shape, indicating that both structures undergo a comparable deformation response during the bending test. Since the energy absorbed by a component during bending is represented by the area under the force–deflection curve, a similar curve profile suggests that the aluminum B-pillar absorbs more energy over the tested deflection range. Therefore, although the materials differ significantly in strength, density, and forming route, the bending results indicate that the aluminum B-pillar can provide an energy absorption level higher to that of the press-hardened steel B-pillar, provided that the comparison is made over the same displacement interval.

sections.heading: Summary and conclusions
paragraphs: Figure  28  depicts a diagram of the 7075 aluminum alloy hot stamping technology. The thermoplastic treatment parameters used while manufacturing the U-shaped element were verified during the production of the entire B-pillar. The developed hot-forming technology enabled the production of a defect-free 7075 aluminum alloy B-pillar with mechanical properties and crashworthiness suitable for automotive body applications. The main findings are summarized as follows:
Fig. 28 Hot forming technology for 7075 aluminum alloy

The initial temperature was equal to 500 °C and the holding time was 45 min (the solutioning start temperature 475 °C is the minimum value for the large area of the B-pillar − 1 m long). The time increase allows for obtaining a homogeneous temperature in the entire volume of the blank. The preheated blank must be immediately transported to the stamping station. Considering that the aluminum air cooling rate is 1–2 °C/s, the transfer time of the blank preheated in the furnace to 500 °C should not exceed 10–15 s. The optimal solutioning temperature was determined to be 475 °C. This temperature is high enough to obtain properties close to the T6 temper after artificial aging, while preventing local overheating and melting of low-melting phases at grain boundaries. A higher solutioning temperature of 530 °C caused brittle intercrystalline cracking due to local melting of grain-boundary phases. Only heat-resistant lubricants should be used for forming (for example multidtraw SHF431) and the tool’s temperature cannot exceed 90 °C. Tests performed on U-shaped elements showed that the temperature of the forming tools strongly affects the final mechanical properties. Tools with temperatures up to 90 °C allowed sufficient supersaturation and, after artificial aging, resulted in tensile strength above 560 MPa and hardness above 169 HV1. When the tool temperature exceeded 90 °C, incomplete supersaturation occurred, leading to lower strength and hardness after aging. Although cooling rates above 30 °C/s were obtained, the initial blank temperature, contact time with the tools, final cooling temperature, and local heat-transfer conditions must also be considered. If the tool’s temperature exceeds 90 °C during serial production, a tool’s cooling system must be additionally used. During the stamping trials of U-shaped elements and the serial production of B-pillars, the tools made of 1.2738HH steel grade did not get hotter than 90 °C. Technological tests (B-pillar forming) allowed for overcoming the problem of aluminum alloy cracking and folding by selecting the appropriate clamping forces. An upper counterstamp pressure of 3 bars should be used to prevent wrinkling. A bottom blankholder pressure of 0.5 bars and a starting position of 31 mm above the lower tool’s surface are also required to speed up the cooling of the hot sheet. It was also proven that surface scuffing could be significantly reduced when the ester oil-based lubricant (Multidraw SHF 431) is combined with the TiCN-based coating of the working surface of the tools. As a result, the roughness of the finished product surface was below Ra = 0.5 μm, which allowed for further preparation of a homogeneous and durable protective coating using the cataphoretic painting process. After simultaneous supersaturation and stamping, the material has a hardness of 90–95 HV1 (due to dissolving all strengthening particles - Fig.  2 ). Within 3 h (before natural aging starts) material should be artificially aged at 120 °C for 8 h [ 50 ]. After such treatment, the product will gain strength above 560 MPa and the crashworthiness of a 3 mm thick aluminum pillar is higher than that of a 1.5 mm thick steel pillar. Structural tests confirmed the presence of MgZn 2  particles strongly strengthening the areas at the highest risk of non-saturation (side and flange of the B-pillar). Additionally, the geometry measurement confirmed that the geometry deviations of crucial areas are within the acceptable range of ± 1 mm. The quasi-static three-point bending test showed that the 3-mm-thick 7075 aluminum B-pillar achieved higher stiffness and higher maximum crushing force than the 1.5-mm-thick hot-stamped 22MnB5 steel B-pillar. The aluminum pillar also maintained plastic deformation over a larger deflection range, while the steel pillar lost stability earlier and fractured in the central area.

Based on the available literature, no reported cases have been identified of a hot stamping technology for the 7075 alloy that enables obtaining a product meeting the required strength, quality, and geometric criteria. Literature reports indicate that previous research has focused solely on the geometry of drawpieces, without taking into account the ultimate strength which is a criterion for the use of the material for car body components. Drawpieces made of 1.6 mm thick aluminum alloy sheet (tested so far) do not demonstrate the same strength or energy absorption as manganese-boron steel. The developed technology (3 mm thick sheet of AA7075) is unique and universal, and the precisely determined parameters of thermo-plastic treatment can be used to produce any complex part of a car body from a high-strength precipitation-hardened aluminum alloy with limited deformation.
